course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 2
unit.description: Follow the Spanish, French, Dutch, and British colonies, the regions of British North America, Atlantic trade, slavery, and colonial society from 1607 to 1754.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

lesson.title: Colonial Society and Culture
lesson.summary: How religious and ethnic diversity, the Great Awakening, Enlightenment ideas, print, and Anglicization shaped colonial culture and prepared colonists to question British control.
learningGoals: Explain how religious and ethnic diversity, the Great Awakening, and the Enlightenment shaped colonial society.
Explain how Anglicization, trade, and print culture tied the colonies to Britain and to each other.
Explain why colonists became dissatisfied with British policies and what ideas supported resistance.
lesson.bigIdea: Diversity, religious revival, Enlightenment ideas, and English political habits bound the colonies to Britain and to each other, even as they gave colonists reasons to resist imperial control.
lesson.context: The CED asks you to explain how the movement of people and ideas across the Atlantic shaped American culture and how colonists viewed their relationship with Britain. Notice what pulled the colonies closer to Britain and what pushed them away.

sections.title: Pluralism and the Great Awakening

blocks.text: The presence of different European religious and ethnic groups, including English Anglicans and Puritans, Dutch Reformed, German Lutherans, Scots-Irish Presbyterians, Quakers, and Catholics, contributed to a significant degree of pluralism and intellectual exchange in the colonies. No single church could claim the loyalty of everyone.

In the 1730s and 1740s the First Great Awakening, a wave of Protestant revivals, swept the colonies. Preachers such as Jonathan Edwards and George Whitefield urged listeners to seek a personal religious experience. Edwards's 1741 sermon "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God" warned that sinners depended on God's mercy. The Awakening divided congregations between supporters and critics, challenged established ministers, increased religious independence and diversity, and gave colonists a shared experience across colonial boundaries.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: The Great Awakening was a religious movement, not a political one, but it taught colonists to question established authority and to organize on their own.

sections.takeaway: Religious and ethnic pluralism, deepened by the Great Awakening, gave colonists more religious independence and common experience.

sections.title: Enlightenment ideas and print culture

blocks.text: The European Enlightenment, an intellectual movement that stressed reason, observation, and natural rights, also spread to the colonies. Benjamin Franklin conducted scientific experiments and helped found the American Philosophical Society in 1743. Colonial readers studied the writings of English thinkers, including John Locke, who argued that government rested on the consent of the governed and existed to protect natural rights.

A transatlantic print culture linked the colonies to Britain and to one another. Colonial newspapers, almanacs, and pamphlets spread news and ideas, and in 1735 a New York jury acquitted the printer John Peter Zenger of libel after he criticized the royal governor, which strengthened ideas about a free press.

sections.takeaway: Enlightenment ideas and a growing print culture connected colonists to Europe and to each other.

sections.title: Anglicization and growing mistrust

blocks.text: Over time the British colonies experienced a gradual Anglicization, developing autonomous political communities based on English models, with elected assemblies, English law, and English customs. Intercolonial commercial ties, the print culture, and the spread of Protestant evangelicalism also helped bind the colonies to Britain and one another.

At the same time, the goals and interests of European leaders and colonists diverged, leading to a growing mistrust on both sides of the Atlantic. Colonists, especially in British North America, were dissatisfied over issues such as territorial settlements, frontier defense, self-rule, and trade. Their resistance drew on local experience of self-government, evolving ideas of liberty, the political thought of the Enlightenment, greater religious independence and diversity, and a belief that the imperial system was corrupt.

sections.takeaway: Colonists became more English in their institutions, yet their experiences and ideas also gave them grounds to resist imperial control.

connections.title: From connection to conflict
connections.body: Unit 3 begins in 1754, when war with France changed the relationship between Britain and its colonies. The habits of self-government and the ideas described here shaped how colonists responded.
connections.transferQuestion: Which of the developments in this topic would most help colonists organize resistance to Britain, and why?
connections.feedback: A strong answer picks one development, such as local self-government, print culture, or the Great Awakening, and explains how it taught colonists to question authority or communicate with each other.
